articles.title: Gujarat: Vadnagar museum becomes first in India to win Red Dot's 'Best of the Best' award
articles.content: Gujarat: Vadnagar museum becomes first in India to win Red Dot’s 'Best of the Best' award IANS November 16, 2026 6:30 PM Share on | Mehsana, Nov 16 (IANS) Gujarat’s Anant Anadi Vadnagar Archaeological Experiential Museum has won the prestigious 'Red Dot: Best of the Best Award 2026' in Berlin, Germany, making it the first and only museum in India to receive the distinction, Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel announced on Monday. Patel said the international recognition placed Vadnagar’s archaeological heritage on the global design map. In a post on social media platform X, he said the museum brought alive the history of a town with more than 2,500 years of uninterrupted human habitation through over 5,000 excavated artefacts and an excavation site that allows visitors to explore different layers of history. "Delighted that Gujarat’s Anant Anadi Vadnagar, the Archaeological Experiential Museum, has won the prestigious Red Dot: Best of the Best Award 2026 in Berlin," the Chief Minister said. He described Vadnagar as a "living testament" to India's civilisational continuity and said the recognition reflected Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of 'Vikas Bhi, Virasat Bhi' (development alongside heritage preservation). Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi also highlighted the achievement on X, saying Vadnagar had made history by receiving the international honour. He said the award had brought Gujarat's heritage to the global design map. "From the timeless legacy of our civilisation to global design excellence, Vadnagar is making history!" Sanghavi said. The museum, located in Vadnagar in Mehsana district, was inaugurated on January 16, 2025, by Union Home Minister Amit Shah. Developed jointly by the Union Ministry of Culture and the Gujarat government, the project was built at a cost of around Rs 298 crore and covers an area of approximately 12,500 square metres. According to the Ministry of Culture, the museum houses nine thematic galleries showcasing Vadnagar's evolution through archaeological discoveries, including pottery, coins, ornaments, weapons, tools, sculptures and other objects. It also displays organic remains, including food grains, DNA samples and skeletal remains, offering insights into the lives and practices of its ancient inhabitants. One of the museum's distinguishing features is its integration with an actual archaeological excavation site. A 4,000-square-metre excavation area, where remains are visible at depths of 16 to 18 metres, is connected to the museum through an experiential walkway, allowing visitors to observe archaeological findings in their original setting. The Red Dot Award's official project description highlights the museum's exhibition design, which uses seven layers of rammed earth to represent different historical periods. It describes the museum's presentation of archaeology as an immersive and participatory journey, with more than 6,000 artefacts serving as narrative elements across 2,500 years of history. The award-winning project was designed by Design Factory India for the state government's Directorate of Archaeology and Museums. The Red Dot: Best of the Best is a distinction within the international Red Dot design awards, recognising outstanding design work. articles.title: Gujarat CM reviews rapid development of Dholera, India's first semiconductor city
articles.content: ANI Photo | Gujarat CM reviews rapid development of Dholera, India’s first semiconductor city Dholera Special Investment Region (DSIR) is accelerating its development as India’s first emerging semiconductor city, with significant progress in industrial growth and the establishment of world-class physical, economic, and social infrastructure. This expansion is creating substantial opportunities for investment in healthcare, hospitality, education, and urban services. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendrabhai Patel recently reviewed key industrial, social, and urban infrastructure projects at Dholera SIR, emphasising the state government’s commitment to fostering a comprehensive ecosystem for businesses, investors, professionals, and residents. ADVERTISEMENT Stay connected Make The News Mill your preferred source See more TNM stories when you search for news on Google. Add TNM on Google During the review, the Chief Minister assessed the advancement of critical social infrastructure within Dholera’s Activation Area. These projects include a 200-bed multi-speciality hospital, an integrated school, a fire station, a hotel, a guest house, a food court, a tent city, and residential and commercial developments. The review highlighted substantial progress since the Chief Minister’s previous visit and confirmed Dholera’s preparedness to become a self-sustained urban and industrial destination. ADVERTISEMENT Hospitality facilities nearing completion include a 42-room guest house featuring suites and conference spaces, a food court with a capacity to serve around 600 people, and a fifty-tent Tent City. These amenities are expected to become operational shortly and will enhance Dholera’s capacity to host investors, industry leaders, business delegations, and visitors from across India and abroad. With large-scale industrial investments underway, demand for quality healthcare and hospitality infrastructure is projected to rise significantly. The forthcoming multi-speciality hospital and hotel projects present attractive opportunities for leading healthcare providers, hospital chains, and hospitality developers aiming to establish an early presence in one of India’s fastest-growing industrial ecosystems. This momentum is driven by the development of the Tata Electronics Semiconductor Fabrication Facility, representing one of India’s most significant semiconductor investments. The plant is anticipated to serve as a hub for a broader semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem, including ancillary industries, technology enterprises, research institutions, skilled professionals, and support services. This development is expected to catalyse demand for robust urban infrastructure and high-quality social amenities. ADVERTISEMENT In parallel with industrial growth, Dholera is advancing sustainability efforts. A large-scale plantation drive, conducted in partnership with the Forest Department and Sadhbhavna Trust, has resulted in the planting of approximately 111,000 saplings over 53 hectares within the Activation Area. Innovative drum plantation techniques have been employed to improve tree survival rates and enhance the city’s green cover, tailored to local climatic conditions. Connectivity infrastructure continues to strengthen Dholera’s attractiveness for investment. The operational Ahmedabad-Dholera Expressway has considerably improved regional access, while the upcoming Dholera International Airport is expected to be operational by the end of 2026, further enhancing domestic and international connectivity. Rail infrastructure is also progressing through strategic projects such as the Bhimnath-Dholera Logistic Hub Rail Line and the Ahmedabad-Dholera Semi High-Speed Double Rail Line. articles.title: AIIMS Delhi Repairs a Baby's Spinal Defect Inside the Womb in India's First Open Foetal Surgery
articles.content: Healthcare Explore all stories ‘14 Years Ago, We Spoke of This Possibility’: How AIIMS Delhi Performed India’s First Open Foetal Surgery to Repair a Baby’s Spine Advertisment At 25 weeks of pregnancy, surgeons at AIIMS opened a mother’s womb to repair her baby’s spine. Over six hours, a team of more than 30 did it, and the pregnancy continued. By Avantika Krishna Edited By Vidya Gowri Venkatesh 16 Nov 2026 At 25 weeks of pregnancy, surgeons at AIIMS opened a mother’s womb to repair her baby’s spine. Over six hours, a team of more than 30 did it, and the pregnancy continued. 16 Nov 2026 18:06 IST Avantika Krishna Follow Us A multidisciplinary team of 37 doctors came together at AIIMS Delhi to perform India's first open foetal spinal surgery. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) On 12 November, a pregnant woman lay on an operating table at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in New Delhi while surgeons performed something no Indian hospital had done before. Advertisment Stories Visual Stories Over six hours, they repaired a gap in her unborn baby’s spine at 25 weeks of pregnancy , then closed the womb so that the pregnancy could continue. Advertisment Add The Better India As A Trusted Source The institute announced on 14 November that this was India’s first open foetal repair of a lumbosacral myelomeningocele, the most severe form of spina bifida. Professor Deepak Gupta, who led the neurosurgical component and is president of the Indian Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery, says, “It establishes an important new capability for foetal care and paediatric neurosurgery in India.” Why doctors operate before birth In myelomeningocele, part of the spinal cord and its protective coverings pushes out through an opening in the spine. Doctors usually close it after the baby is born, but the institute said that exposure to amniotic fluid during pregnancy can cause progressive neurological injury. Surgeons used microsurgical techniques and ultrasound guidance to repair an unborn baby's spinal defect inside the womb. Photograph: ( TNIE ) “Affected children can develop paralysis or hydrocephalus, a build-up of fluid in the brain,” the team says. In open foetal surgery , the surgeons open the mother’s uterus to reach the defect, then carefully repair and cover the exposed spinal tissue in layers using microsurgical techniques before closing the uterus and abdomen, which lets the pregnancy continue under close supervision. Five weeks of rehearsal for one operation The operation followed more than five weeks of preparation that included detailed foetal imaging, counselling of the parents, anaesthetic planning and surgical simulations. “More than 30 doctors, specialists and nurses then took part, drawn from obstetrics, maternal-foetal medicine, neurosurgery, anaesthesia, plastic surgery, radiodiagnosis and neonatology, working with high-end microscopy and continuous ultrasound guidance at the Neurosciences Centre,” the team says. More than five weeks of preparation and surgical simulations preceded the six-hour operation at AIIMS Delhi. articles.title: Sophrosyne Technologies Successfully Completes Post-Silicon Validation of India's first ...
articles.content: Sophrosyne Technologies Successfully Completes Post-Silicon Validation of India’s first Biomedical Sensor Chipset for Wearable Health Monitoring The milestone marks a significant step towards developing homegrown semiconductor technology for next-generation healthcare and wearable applications. The chipset demonstrates ultra-low-power performance, high-precision analog capabilities and successful capture of the first live ECG signal using indigenous silicon. The company is now progressing towards a commercial-ready version of the chipset and potential proof-of-concept engagements with leading wearable device brands. Sophrosyne Technologies, an Indian deep-tech semiconductor company, has successfully completed the post-silicon validation of the first version of its indigenous biomedical sensor chipset, developed specifically for wearable-based health monitoring. The achievement marks an important milestone in the company's journey towards building homegrown semiconductor solutions at the intersection of healthcare, artificial intelligence and advanced chip design. Developed through extensive research and engineering efforts, the chipset integrates ultra-low-power, high-precision analog designs and proprietary intellectual property (IP) innovations. During the validation process, the team successfully demonstrated the chip's capabilities in vital-sign acquisition and captured its first live electrocardiogram (ECG) signal using its own silicon. The results have been encouraging, demonstrating the potential of the technology for next-generation wearable health monitoring applications. The successful validation follows months of dedicated engineering and chip development. Having taped out the design in late April 2026, the company has now received the fabricated silicon and completed the initial validation of its first chipset version. Advancing India's Indigenous Semiconductor Capabilities The development represents a positive step towards strengthening India's capabilities in designing and developing specialised semiconductor technology for healthcare applications. As wearable devices increasingly become part of everyday health and fitness monitoring, purpose-built chips with efficient power consumption and high-precision sensing capabilities can play an important role in enabling more advanced and reliable solutions. Sophrosyne Technologies is working towards building an indigenous technology platform that can support the next generation of wearable-based health monitoring devices, contributing to India's growing semiconductor and health-tech ecosystem. The company acknowledges the support and encouragement received from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), the DLI Technical Committee,C-DAC team and Bluehill VC during its development journey. The achievement also reflects the collaborative efforts of its engineering team and technical experts who contributed to bringing the chipset from design to silicon validation. Taking the Technology Towards Commercialisation Building on this milestone, Sophrosyne Technologies is now focusing on developing the commercial-ready version of its chipset. Over the next 10 months, the company plans to progress towards its next tape-out and initiate proof-of-concept (PoC) engagements with leading Indian and global wearable device brands. With growing interest from potential customers and encouraging early engagement around its technology, the company aims to take its indigenous semiconductor innovation closer to commercial applications in India and international markets. Through this development, Sophrosyne Technologies is contributing to the evolution of India's deep-tech ecosystem, demonstrating the growing potential of homegrown semiconductor innovation to support emerging applications across healthcare, wearables and connected technologies. articles.title: Smart AI Navigation Enables India's First Day Care Bilateral Hip Replacement at Max Super ...
articles.content: Smart AI Navigation Enables India's First Day Care Bilateral Hip Replacement at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket 40-year-old patient undergoes robot assisted total replacement of both hips joints in a single sitting and discharged from the hospital on the same day Doctors at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, have performed India's first day care bilateral total hip replacement using Smart AI Navigation technology. The 40-year-old patient from Myanmar underwent replacement of both hip joints in a single surgical session and was discharged from the hospital on the same day. The procedure was performed by a team led by Dr. Sujoy Bhattacharjee, Chairman & Chief, Max Institute of Robotic Joint Replacement. Patients who require both hip replacement usually stay in hospital for several days for monitoring, pain management and rehabilitation. In this case, the team achieved early mobilisation and same-day discharge by combining navigation-assisted surgery, meticulous preoperative planning and an enhanced recovery protocol. The patient, Mr. Juya Mani, had avascular necrosis (AVN) of both hips, a condition in which reduced blood supply causes the bone to deteriorate. He had lived with pain in both hips for many years, which had become markedly worse over the past few months, particularly on the right, and had progressively restricted his ability to walk. After a detailed clinical and radiological evaluation at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, he was admitted under the care of Dr. Sujoy Bhattacharjee for surgery. Both hips were replaced with uncemented implants from the Meril Libertas Hip Replacement System. The surgery took approximately 3.5 hours, and the patient was mobilised under medical supervision within four hours of being shifted to the recovery room. Once he had met the clinical and functional discharge criteria, he went home the same day with medication, postoperative care instructions and a structured rehabilitation plan. Commenting on the milestone, Dr. Bhattacharjee said, “Replacing both hips in one sitting normally means a longer hospital stay for monitoring and rehabilitation. Smart AI Navigation gave us precise implant positioning and alignment, and with careful planning and a structured recovery protocol we were able to mobilise the patient early and send him home safely the same day. This is an important step forward for day care joint replacement. It shows that, in carefully selected patients, same-day discharge is possible even after a bilateral procedure.” Navigation-assisted hip replacement uses advanced surgical planning and computer guidance to help the surgeon position implants according to each patient's anatomy. The surgeon remains in control throughout, while the technology improves precision in implant placement and alignment. Bilateral hip replacement is generally recommended for patients with advanced disease in both hips, such as severe osteoarthritis or avascular necrosis. Replacing both joints in one sitting avoids second operation and a second anaesthetic, and the patient goes through a single period of rehabilitation. The case shows how navigation-assisted surgery and enhanced recovery protocols can shorten hospital stays and support early rehabilitation in carefully selected patients undergoing complex joint replacement. articles.title: 'Tokeniser tax': Why AI is more expensive for non-English users - Scroll.in
articles.content: Via Unsplash This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West. People who use less widely spoken languages could end up paying more to use artificial intelligence than those who speak English or other dominant languages. A new study published last month by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found AI models require far more tokens for some languages than others. Tokens are the units of text or data that the models process. The researchers have called this a hidden “tokeniser tax,” which can make AI more expensive in languages with smaller online presence. A tokeniser is a tool that breaks down raw text, images, or audio into tokens. Tokenisation example. A graphic representation of the tokenisation of the sentence “People should benefit from AI, regardless of the language they speak.”in English and Malayalam using The OpenAI tokeniser API (https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer) . The English sentence gets split into recognisable words, while the Malayalam sentence gets multiple fragments per word without respect for multi-byte characters Even within the 20 most popular languages on the internet, there is a gap in token usage, the research found. The most expensive of the languages used between 1.5 and 5 times more tokens than the cheapest. This gap widened when researchers expanded the set to 200 languages, with the token cost gap in one AI model growing by 17 times. Advertisement “A startup in [Bengaluru] may pay a surcharge on every prompt and completion while its competitor in Austin does not,” the study said. “The tokeniser tax also has implications beyond cost. Higher token counts translate into higher latency and reduced effective context capacity. These penalties hit hardest where compute and connectivity are already limited. Tokeniser inequity is a constraint on who can participate in the AI economy.” Non-English languages leave less room for documents or conversation history, and require more work to generate the answer, according to Pratyush Choudhury, co-founder of Activate AI, India’s first venture capital fund dedicated exclusively to AI. Activate backs multilingual voice AI startups like ElevenLabs, Sarvam, and Wispr Flow. “Think about a tutor: Retaining the student’s earlier mistakes and explanations is part of delivering a good lesson. If that history consumes the context window much faster in one language, the disadvantage reaches into the quality of the service,” he said. Advertisement One way to improve language processing is to improve the underlying data. “Open data efforts matter here, like RESPIN, a collaborative initiative with [the Indian Institute of Science] funded by the Gates Foundation, where we collected text from native speakers of 38 dialects along with read speech,” Raoul Nanavati, co-founder and CEO of Mumbai-based AI voice infrastructure startup Navana.ai , told Rest of World . articles.title: Cold Calling: Film chronicles how scientists braved extreme conditions to build India's first ...
articles.content: Braving the icy desert of Antarctica, around 43 years ago, a team of 81 Indian scientists, Army, Navy and Air Force personnel achieved something that had never been done before or since then: building a permanent research station in one Antarctic summer, a period of six months. “No country, including the US, Russia or China, had achieved what these guys were proposing on this trip. Permanent stations used to be built little by little over years, but there are multiple problems with that; it’s inefficient and sometimes, the previous years’ gets undone because of the ice. So it was an onerous task and they were given only a 15 per cent chance of success by experts. But they prevailed against all odds,” says filmmaker Santosh Saligram. He and collaborator Sourabha Rao, screened their documentary Miracle in Antarctica chronicling this historic feat in Indian science history, at BLR Design Centre, Church Street, on Sunday. The station, built the same year as India signed the Antarctic Treaty, was India’s third expedition to the continent and was crucial because a permanent research station meant that Indian scientists could stay to continue their research throughout the inhospitable winter months. “Twelve nations had already signed the Antarctic Treaty which denounced any activity in Antarctica other than science and research. India wanted to be taken seriously in its capabilities in science and research, and share international space in the Antarctic discussion,” explains Saligram. At the core of the documentary are interviews with three scientists: Harsh Kumar Gupta who led the mission, KJ Mathew and Ashok Hanjura, along with a few conversations with their family and friends, helping paint a picture of the people at the core of the mission. This was important to the duo since the project was born out of Gupta’s search for someone to do justice to the story, after being put off by Bollywood sensationalism, notes Rao, adding, “One part of the story is the science but the other is the scientists as people.” Avoiding sensationalism doesn’t mean the story of the expedition has any dearth of excitement though, with Saligram sharing that one incident that kept resurfacing across interviews was a close brush with death soon after the scientists’ ship reached the Antarctic ice wall. “M18 helicopters were being used to transport cargo inland from the ship. On the third day, the helicopter crashed into the water and the five people inside had to break the plexiglass window at the bottom to escape,” he says, continuing, “While being rescued by a second helicopter, two people caught hold of the rope but did not sling it properly. Because their hands must have been freezing, they fell into the water again from a great height. You can actually see this in the footage in the documentary. It’s utterly terrifying. Eventually, they were rescued by a lifeboat, but because they were all scattered in different places, some came really close to knocking on death’s door because of hypothermia.” Another moment that stands out to...
